items.title: 68113_Barney Bigard oral history interview
items.q: And so George told me, "Get here a little early because Duke is coming in early."

ctx.x: No, '73, I guess it must have been because he died in '74. It must have been 1973.

Well, -- which was George Wein's idea that he'd like to reminisce, you know, get a few of his men that was in the group, like Sonny, Nance, myself, and somebody else, I don't know. And so George told me, "Get here a little early because Duke is coming in early." He had been working somewhere. I don't know, it was somewhere in Jersey somewhere. And he was coming in for a rehearsal with Nance and Sonny and myself. And so I said, "Okay."

So I came in early and there he was. So he started rehearsing things that he had been playing, I mean, probably all that night. So he said, "What you want to do?" I said, "I'll do something simple." He said, "How about 'Tiger Rag'?" I said, "You must be kidding. 'Tiger Rag'. It's hard. I said simple. Don't you know what simple means?" So he said, "What?" I said, "Rose Room." I said, "Everybody knows 'Rose Room.'" So he said, "Okay." He said, "What tempo?" I said, "You know the right tempo," and I gave him the…

items.title: George Wein — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Barney Bigard was the clarinet and Jack Teagarden, trombone player, Cozy Cole on drums, Earl Fatha Hines on the piano.

ctx.x: Well, Mrs. Donnelley who owned the Club Sade [Mrs. Donahue owned the Savoy] and I knew the musicians and why not do that. And I did that successfully. That was a good thing for about a month or two, I don't know. I brought in Vic Dickenson and I brought in Wild Bill, I brought in Joe Thomas, a wonderful trumpet player, and with local musicians, and I was playing piano. We had some good weeks there. But I think when Phil Napoleon came in with his own band and sold Mrs. Donahue the idea of having his band – which…

night. One night – and Bob Wilber as the opener – and I asked Bob but he a different kind of band. He had Wilber and Sidney de Paris and Big Sid Catlett on the drums. And of course having Big Sid there was … that was a thrill. But I mean, that band cost me a thousand dollars a week. That's a lot of money. Six guys living in New York, paying their hotels … and getting a thousand dollars a week. Maybe it wasn't a thousand, maybe it was nine hundred. One night Louis Armstrong and the All-Stars were playing at…
[NOTE TO KIMERY re above and elsewhere– George refers to Pops as Louie, rather than Louis. Don't know if/how that should be handled. George does the same re Louie/Louis Lorillard.]
